claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi by removing Co.
The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy initially has an as-solidified, single-phase solid-solution structure.
Removing Co lowers the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes a transition from classical dislocation glide toward deformation twinning.
Dynamic strain aging may become active in the Co-free alloy at moderate temperatures and strain rates.
The relevant regime is above room temperature but below temperatures at which recovery dominates.
Within that regime, the Co-free alloy will develop a higher deformation-twin density than CoCrFeMnNi.
The Co-free alloy will exhibit altered dislocation arrangements or other microstructural signatures of dynamic strain aging.
Greater deformation twinning enhances work hardening and contributes to favorable strength and ductility.
The proposed mechanism transition will give the Co-free alloy a higher work-hardening rate and superior strength–ductility balance relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Dislocation glide is the dominant deformation mechanism in the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
Differences between the two alloys will diminish at very high strain rates or low temperatures.
Differences between the two alloys will diminish at temperatures high enough for extensive recovery or recrystallization.
Controlled tensile testing of both alloys across temperature and strain-rate ranges, coupled with twin and dislocation characterization, can distinguish the proposed mechanism.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in twin density or dynamic-strain-aging evidence together with increased work hardening in the Co-free alloy would falsify the proposed mechanism.
